what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus), the virus that can cause AIDS. It contains two antiviral medicines that work together to lower the amount of HIV in your blood. This helps your immune system stay stronger and reduces your risk of getting infections. This medicine does NOT cure HIV, but it helps control it.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with or without food. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablet unless your doctor tells you to. Wash your hands before and after handling the tablet. Keep taking this medicine even if you feel well — stopping without talking to your doctor can make the virus harder to treat.
dosing: The usual adult dose is ONE tablet taken TWICE a day — once in the morning and once in the evening, about 12 hours apart. Each tablet contains 150 mg of lamivudine and 300 mg of zidovudine. Your doctor may prescribe a different dose if you have kidney or liver problems. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do NOT take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. Try setting a phone alarm or pill reminder to help you remember your doses every day.
storage: Store at room temperature between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in a dry place away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do NOT store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase the risk of serious liver problems. Avoid taking other medicines that contain lamivudine or zidovudine to prevent accidental double-dosing. Do not take stavudine (d4T) along with this medicine, as the combination can be harmful. Do not share this medicine with anyone else — even if they also have HIV. Always tell all your doctors, dentists, and pharmacists that you are taking this medicine before starting any new medicines, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements. HIV can still be passed to others even while you are on treatment, so continue to use protection during sex and do not share needles.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: severe nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or loss of appetite (these can be signs of lactic acidosis or liver problems); yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual muscle pain or weakness; trouble breathing or feeling short of breath; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing; unusual tiredness or weakness; pale skin, fast heartbeat, or dizziness (signs of anemia — low red blood cells); fever, chills, or other signs of infection; numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet; dark-colored urine or very light-colored stools. Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away to reduce the amount of HIV in your blood, but it may take several weeks to months before your blood tests (called viral load and CD4 counts) show significant improvement. Most people start to feel better gradually as the medicine helps protect their immune system. It is very important to keep taking this medicine every day as directed, even when you feel well, because stopping or skipping doses can allow the virus to multiply and become resistant to the medicine.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine is sometimes used during pregnancy to reduce the risk of passing HIV to your baby, but your doctor needs to carefully monitor you. There is a small risk of a serious condition called lactic acidosis in pregnant women using this combination. BREASTFEEDING: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. HIV can be passed to your baby through breast milk. CHILDREN: This medicine is generally not recommended for children who weigh less than 66 pounds (30 kg) because the dose cannot be easily adjusted. Ask your child's doctor about appropriate alternatives. KIDNEY PROBLEMS: If you have moderate to severe kidney disease, your doctor may need to prescribe separate medicines at adjusted doses instead of this combination tablet. LIVER PROBLEMS: Use with caution if you have liver disease. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Tell your doctor if you have hepatitis B, as stopping this medicine suddenly can cause a serious flare-up of hepatitis B. ELDERLY PATIENTS: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially anemia and kidney-related issues. Your doctor will monitor you carefully.
